# Testing optic-flow and vectorial predictions in marching locusts

How do moving neighbours influence a locust's choice of direction? This notebook reanalyses a virtual-reality experiment from [Sayin et al. (2025), *The behavioral mechanisms governing collective motion in swarming locusts*](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adq7832). Juvenile desert locusts walked on a motion-compensating ball while viewing virtual neighbours on either side. The arrangement separates two predictions: an optic-flow account predicts continued forward movement, whereas a vectorial account predicts movement toward one of the two lateral groups.

We express headings relative to the experimental forward direction. Forward is $0$ radians; the two lateral directions are $-\pi/2$ and $+\pi/2$, or $-90^\circ$ and $+90^\circ$. These are the directions at which we later evaluate the fitted model. The model's preferred directions are estimated from the observations.

The full distribution of headings matters here. Two strong preferences in opposite directions can cancel in a circular mean, concealing a structured pattern. A mixture of von Mises distributions can describe two directional tendencies while allowing animals to differ in their preferred directions, concentration, and relative use of the two components.

The analysis asks three connected questions: does allowing two components improve prediction of another heading; do fitted models reproduce the observed directional pattern; and how much density does the fitted mixture assign to the directions predicted by each account? Keeping these questions separate makes the biological interpretation of each figure clearer.

## Reading the figures

Orange identifies the two-component fit and blue the single-component fit in the comparison figures. Red shows the fitted mixture density in the analytic-density figures. Black observations and bootstrap summaries provide the empirical comparison. The captions and section text distinguish uncertainty in a fitted density from variation among replicated heading datasets.


## From trajectories to headings

The recordings are converted into successive displacements of approximately six body lengths, or 0.24 m. The bearing of each displacement supplies one heading for the analysis. Successive points are selected by their straight-line separation, so this is a distance-based representation of movement rather than a series of measurements at fixed time intervals. Using these displacements reduces the duplication inherent in densely sampled positions; it does not establish that all dependence between successive headings has disappeared.

Of 54 recordings, two yield no qualifying displacements. The analysed dataset therefore contains 2,435 headings from 52 locusts. Headings are measured in radians on the circle, with $-\pi$ and $+\pi$ representing the same direction. The data come from [the accompanying data repository](https://github.com/jgraving/unwrap-data).
Animals contribute between 3 and 204 headings. Consequently, a detailed directional distribution is much better informed for some animals than for others. The hierarchical model shares information across animals while retaining individual differences: estimates for sparsely observed animals depend more strongly on the shared population structure. A broad interval for an individual can reflect limited information as well as variation in its headings.

```{r}
  if (!dir.exists(target)) {
    if (!dir.exists(data_root)) {
      status <- system2("git", c("clone", "--depth", "1",
        "--filter=blob:none", "--sparse",
        "https://github.com/jgraving/unwrap-data.git", shQuote(data_root)))
      if (status != 0L) stop("Could not fetch the published study data.")
    }
    # Sparse checkout downloads only this study; later notebooks may add
    # their own subdirectory to the same checkout without replacing it.
    status <- system2("git", c("-C", shQuote(data_root),
                              "sparse-checkout", "add", subdir))
    if (status != 0L) stop("Could not materialize the study subdirectory.")
  }
  stopifnot(dir.exists(target))
  target
}
```

## A hierarchical mixture for individual heading distributions

For animal $i$, the two-component model describes a heading $y$ by

$$
f_i(y)=\omega_i\,\mathcal M(y\mid\mu_{i,1},\kappa_{i,1})
 +(1-\omega_i)\,\mathcal M(y\mid\mu_{i,2},\kappa_{i,2}),
$$

where each component is a normalized von Mises density,

$$
\mathcal M(y\mid\mu,\kappa)
=\frac{\exp\{\kappa\cos(y-\mu)\}}{2\pi I_0(\kappa)}.
$$

Here $I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of order zero. The mean direction $\mu$ locates a component around the circle, and its concentration $\kappa$ controls how tightly headings cluster around that direction. Small concentration produces a broad distribution; larger concentration produces a narrower peak. The weight $\omega_i$ gives the modeled share of animal $i$'s headings associated with the first component, with $1-\omega_i$ assigned to the second.

These parameters separate three biological features: where an animal tends to head, how consistently it heads there, and how much it uses each directional tendency. The weights describe the distribution within an animal; they do not divide the animals into two permanent groups. One component can dominate for an individual, and overlapping or diffuse components need not produce two distinct visible peaks.

### Sharing information across animals

Each animal has its own parameters, related to shared population parameters through individual deviations:

$$
\mu_{i,k}=\operatorname{wrap}(\mu_{0,k}+b_{i,k}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{softplus}^{-1}(\kappa_{i,k})
=\operatorname{softplus}^{-1}(\kappa_{0,k})+a_{i,k},
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\omega_i)
=\operatorname{logit}(\omega_0)+c_i.
$$

Wrapping keeps mean directions on the circle. The softplus function, $\operatorname{softplus}(x)=\log(1+e^x)$, keeps concentration positive; the inverse-logit keeps the weight between zero and one. Angular deviations have von Mises distributions centred on zero, and concentration and weight deviations have zero-centred Gaussian distributions on their respective transformed scales. The strengths of these distributions govern how much individuals can depart from the shared pattern.

The concentration governing variation in individual mean directions has a different role from $\kappa_{i,k}$. The former describes variation between animals; the latter describes variation in headings within an animal and component. This distinction allows animals to differ in their preferences without treating all their headings as one undifferentiated sample.

Conditional on its parameters, an animal's headings contribute independently to the likelihood:

$$
p(Y\mid\Theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M_i}f_i(y_{i,j}).
$$

This is a modeling assumption about the preprocessed headings. The hierarchy accounts for shared animal-specific parameters; it does not explicitly model remaining temporal dependence.

Setting all individual deviations to zero defines the population reference mixture $f_0$. Later figures distinguish this reference from averages over the observed animals and from predictions that would integrate over the individual variation of a new animal.

The population direction priors are nearly uniform, so the two means can be learned without fixing them at the theory-predicted angles. Component numbers are bookkeeping labels. The implementation orders the population angles and applies the same permutation to all associated component parameters, leaving the mixture density unchanged. That ordering does not guarantee continuous component identities across the angular boundary or establish that sampling has converged.


### Priors and partial pooling

The priors describe plausible variation before observing the headings. The almost uniform population-angle priors allow preferred directions anywhere on the circle. Angular pooling concentration controls how much animals' component directions can differ from their population direction. The remaining scale priors govern variation between animals in concentration and component use. The table records the specifications for both fits; their pooling and concentration priors differ as well as their component counts.

| Quantity | Bimodal prior | Unimodal prior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Population angle(s) | VM(0, 0.000001), two independent | VM(0, 0.000001) |
| Angular pooling concentration | LogNormal(log(30), 0.1), per component | LogNormal(log(30), 0.1) |
| Animal angular deviation | VM(0, component pooling concentration) | VM(0, pooling concentration) |
| Population pre-softplus concentration | Normal(log(exp(2)-1), 0.5), per component | Normal(log(exp(2)-1), 0.5) |
| Concentration deviation scale | HalfNormal(1.5), per component | HalfNormal(1.5) |
| Standardized concentration deviations | Normal(0, 1), independent | Normal(0, 1), independent |
| Population weight logit | Normal(0, 0.5) | — |
| Weight-logit deviation scale | HalfNormal(3) | — |
| Standardized weight-logit deviations | Normal(0, 1), independent | — |

Partial pooling is especially useful for animals with few observations, whose individual parameters are weakly informed by their own headings. It also makes the prior assumptions consequential for those animals. The fitted individual uncertainty should therefore be read alongside both the observation counts and the shared population pattern.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-017"
locust_mix <- custom_family("locust_mix",
  dpars = c("mu", "mutwo", "kappa", "kappatwo", "eta"),
  links = c("identity", "identity", "softplus", "softplus", "identity"),
  lb = c(NA, NA, 0, 0, NA), vars = "first_component", type = "real")
locust_vm <- custom_family("locust_vm", dpars = c("mu", "kappa"),
  links = c("identity", "softplus"), lb = c(NA, 0), type = "real")
vm_functions <- modulo_circular_fun + stan_unwrap_fun + stanvar(scode = "
  real locust_wrap(real x) {
    return atan2(sin(x), cos(x));
  }
  real locust_vm_lpdf(real y, real mu, real kappa) {
    return unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(y | locust_wrap(mu), kappa);
  }
  real unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(vector y, real mu, real kappa) {
    real lp = 0;
    for (i in 1:num_elements(y)) lp += unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(y[i] | mu, kappa);
    return lp;
  }
", block = "functions")
mix_functions <- stanvar(scode = "
  real locust_mix_lpdf(real y, real mu, real mutwo, real kappa,
                       real kappatwo, real eta, real first_component) {
    array[2] real means = {mu, mutwo};
    array[2] real concentrations = {kappa, kappatwo};
    int first = first_component == 1 ? 1 : 2;
    int second = 3 - first;
    real sorted_eta = first == 1 ? eta : -eta;
    return log_sum_exp(
      log_inv_logit(sorted_eta) +
        unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(y | locust_wrap(means[first]), concentrations[first]),
      log_inv_logit(-sorted_eta) +
        unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(y | locust_wrap(means[second]), concentrations[second]));
  }
", block = "functions")
# A parameter-dependent order belongs in transformed parameters. Stan
# stores the first index as a real; the likelihood reconstructs the two
# integer indices locally. This is Python's argsort for two angles.
mix_order <- stanvar(scode = "
  real first_component = b_popone[1] <= b_poptwo[1] ? 1 : 2;
", block = "tparameters")
mix_hyper <- stanvar(scode = "real<lower=0> kmu_one; real<lower=0> kmu_two;",
                     block = "parameters")
# All animal coefficient vectors have the same level order, 0..51.
mix_form <- bf(direction ~ mu,
  nlf(mu ~ popone + devone),
  nlf(mutwo ~ poptwo + devtwo),
  popone ~ 1, poptwo ~ 1,
  devone ~ 0 + animal, devtwo ~ 0 + animal,
  kappa ~ 0 + Intercept + (1 | animal),
  kappatwo ~ 0 + Intercept + (1 | animal),
  eta ~ 0 + Intercept + (1 | animal),
  family = locust_mix)
# Circular component means are UNCONSTRAINED reals; circularity enters only
# through the wrapped (mod 2*pi) von Mises target lines added to the Stan
# code below - the same convention as the Python twin, which declares
# pm.VonMises priors on unwrapped parameters and wraps at use
# (circular_modulo), with no uniform(-pi, pi) bound.
mix_priors <- (
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(b_popone[1] | 0, 1e-6)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(b_poptwo[1] | 0, 1e-6)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_devone | 0, kmu_one)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_devtwo | 0, kmu_two)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += lognormal_lpdf(kmu_one | log(30), 0.1)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += lognormal_lpdf(kmu_two | log(30), 0.1)", check = FALSE) +
  prior("normal(log(exp(2) - 1), 0.5)", class = "b", coef = "Intercept", dpar = "kappa") +
  prior("normal(log(exp(2) - 1), 0.5)", class = "b", coef = "Intercept", dpar = "kappatwo") +
  prior("normal(0, 1.5)", class = "sd", dpar = "kappa") +
  prior("normal(0, 1.5)", class = "sd", dpar = "kappatwo") +
  prior("normal(0, 0.5)", class = "b", coef = "Intercept", dpar = "eta") +
  prior("normal(0, 3)", class = "sd", dpar = "eta")
)

check_angle_design <- function(stan, design, coefficients) {
  parameter_block <- regmatches(stan,
    regexpr("(?m)^parameters\\s*\\{[^}]*\\}", stan, perl = TRUE))
  parameter_block <- gsub("[[:space:]]", "", parameter_block)
  stopifnot(length(parameter_block) == 1L)
  for (name in names(coefficients)) {
    expected <- coefficients[[name]]
    declaration <- paste0("vector\\[K_", name, "\\]b_", name, ";")
    stopifnot(grepl(declaration, parameter_block),
      !grepl("lower=-3\\.14159", parameter_block),
      identical(colnames(design[[paste0("X_", name)]]), expected),
      design[[paste0("K_", name)]] == length(expected))
  }
}
mix_stanvars <- vm_functions + mix_functions + mix_hyper + mix_order
mix_stan <- make_stancode(mix_form, data = df, prior = mix_priors, stanvars = mix_stanvars)
mix_design <- make_standata(mix_form, data = df, prior = mix_priors, stanvars = mix_stanvars)
animal_design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + animal, data = df)
check_angle_design(mix_stan, mix_design,
  list(popone = "Intercept", poptwo = "Intercept",
    devone = colnames(animal_design), devtwo = colnames(animal_design)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mix_design$X_devone, animal_design, check.attributes = FALSE)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(mix_design$X_devtwo, animal_design, check.attributes = FALSE)))
compact_mix_stan <- gsub("[[:space:]]", "", mix_stan)
stopifnot(grepl("first_component=b_popone[1]<=b_poptwo[1]?1:2;", compact_mix_stan, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("target\\+=locust_mix_lpdf\\([^;]+,first_component\\);", compact_mix_stan),
          grepl("unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_devone|0,kmu_one)", compact_mix_stan, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_devtwo|0,kmu_two)", compact_mix_stan, fixed = TRUE))
cat("Bimodal model: Stan code validated -", mix_design$K_popone, "popone +",
    mix_design$K_devone, "devone coefficients, unbounded and wrapped in the",
    "likelihood (no uniform(-pi, pi) prior or bound). \n")

```

### Fitting the two-component model

Bayesian sampling combines the priors and observed headings to produce draws from the posterior distribution. Multiple chains allow us to assess whether sampling consistently explores the same distribution. Initial values place the chains near plausible directions on the circle without fixing the fitted means at those locations. Reliable inference still depends on the resulting diagnostics.

The full fit uses four chains with 4,000 warmup iterations and 4,000 retained draws per chain. Quick mode retains this sampling budget and reduces only the later resampling and predictive simulations. The sampling diagnostics are part of assessing the fit, rather than a check that can be replaced by visually plausible figures.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-019"
set.seed(SEED)
initial_clusters <- kmeans(cbind(cos(df$direction), sin(df$direction)),
                           centers = 2L, nstart = 20L)
cluster_means <- vapply(split(df$direction, initial_clusters$cluster), circ_mean, numeric(1))
cluster_order <- order(cluster_means)
anchor_mix <- as.numeric(mod_circular(cluster_means[cluster_order]))
initial_group <- match(initial_clusters$cluster, cluster_order)
animal_offsets <- function(component) {
  vapply(levels(df$animal), function(id) {
    y <- df$direction[df$animal == id & initial_group == component]
    if (!length(y)) 0 else mod_circular(circ_mean(y) - anchor_mix[component])
  }, numeric(1))
}
anchor_offsets_one <- animal_offsets(1L)
anchor_offsets_two <- animal_offsets(2L)
stopifnot(length(anchor_mix) == mix_design$K_popone + mix_design$K_poptwo,
          length(anchor_offsets_one) == mix_design$K_devone,
          length(anchor_offsets_two) == mix_design$K_devtwo,
          all(abs(anchor_mix) < pi - 0.2),
          all(abs(c(anchor_offsets_one, anchor_offsets_two)) < pi - 0.5))
mk_init <- function(anchor_seed) {
  set.seed(anchor_seed)
  j <- function(n) runif(n, -0.08, 0.08)
  list(b_popone = as.numeric(anchor_mix[1] + j(mix_design$K_popone)),
       b_poptwo = as.numeric(anchor_mix[2] + j(mix_design$K_poptwo)),
       b_devone = as.numeric(anchor_offsets_one + j(mix_design$K_devone)),
       b_devtwo = as.numeric(anchor_offsets_two + j(mix_design$K_devtwo)))
}
init_mix <- lapply(seq_len(CHAINS), function(k) mk_init(SEED + k))
set.seed(SEED)
# Fit-cache name is versioned (unbounded): the v1 model constrained the
# circular coefficients to (-pi, pi) with uniform priors; this model does not.
fit_bimodal <- unwrap_load_fit_cache("locust_mix_bimodal_unbounded", SEED, ITER, WARMUP)
if (is.null(fit_bimodal)) {
  fit_bimodal <- brm(mix_form, data = df, prior = mix_priors, stanvars = mix_stanvars,
    backend = "cmdstanr", chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP,
    cores = CHAINS, seed = SEED, init = init_mix,
    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.97, max_treedepth = 12))
  unwrap_save_fit_cache("locust_mix_bimodal_unbounded", fit_bimodal, SEED, ITER, WARMUP)
}
```

```{r}
chain_matrix <- function(x, draws) {
  stopifnot(length(x) == nrow(draws))
  ids <- split(seq_len(nrow(draws)), draws[[".chain"]])
  stopifnot(length(ids) >= 2L, length(unique(lengths(ids))) == 1L)
  do.call(cbind, lapply(ids, function(ii) x[ii[order(draws[[".iteration"]][ii])]]))
}
state_bimodal <- extract_state(fit_bimodal)
summary_bimodal <- diagnose_fit(fit_bimodal, state_bimodal)
```

## A one-component comparison

We also fit a hierarchical von Mises model with one preferred direction and one concentration for each animal:

$$
f_i(y)=\mathcal M(y\mid\mu_i,\kappa_i).
$$

This model asks how much of the pattern can be explained by a single directional tendency within each animal, allowing individuals to have different preferences. Averaging such animals can itself produce two peaks at the population level. The more specific question is whether allowing two components within each animal improves the description and prediction of its headings.

The single-component mean is freely estimated, including its population mean. It is not constrained to the forward prediction. Likewise, the mixture's means are not fixed to the lateral predictions. The theory names attached to some figure labels therefore serve as shorthand; the fitted one- and two-component models are not complete mechanistic models of optic flow and vectorial encoding. Their concentration and pooling priors also differ, so their comparison concerns the fitted specifications as a whole.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-023"
uni_hyper <- stanvar(scode = "real<lower=0> kmu_one;", block = "parameters")
uni_form <- bf(direction ~ mu,
  nlf(mu ~ popone + devone),
  popone ~ 1, devone ~ 0 + animal,
  kappa ~ 0 + Intercept + (1 | animal), family = locust_vm)
# Unconstrained circular parameters + wrapped (mod 2*pi) von Mises Stan
# target lines, mirroring the Python unimodal twin (pm.VonMises prior on an
# unwrapped parameter, wrapped via circular_modulo at use).
uni_priors <- (
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_lpdf(b_popone[1] | 0, 1e-6)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_devone | 0, kmu_one)", check = FALSE) +
  set_prior("target += lognormal_lpdf(kmu_one | log(30), 0.1)", check = FALSE) +
  prior("normal(log(exp(2) - 1), 0.5)", class = "b", coef = "Intercept", dpar = "kappa") +
  prior("normal(0, 1.5)", class = "sd", dpar = "kappa")
)
uni_stanvars <- vm_functions + uni_hyper
uni_stan <- make_stancode(uni_form, data = df, prior = uni_priors, stanvars = uni_stanvars)

uni_design <- make_standata(uni_form, data = df, prior = uni_priors, stanvars = uni_stanvars)
check_angle_design(uni_stan, uni_design,
  list(popone = "Intercept", devone = colnames(animal_design)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(uni_design$X_devone, animal_design, check.attributes = FALSE)))
compact_uni_stan <- gsub("[[:space:]]", "", uni_stan)
stopifnot(grepl("target+=locust_vm_lpdf", compact_uni_stan, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("unwrap_von_mises_vect_lpdf(b_devone|0,kmu_one)", compact_uni_stan, fixed = TRUE),
          grepl("lognormal_lpdf(kmu_one|log(30),0.1)", compact_uni_stan, fixed = TRUE))
cat("Unimodal model: Stan code validated -", uni_design$K_popone, "popone +",
    uni_design$K_devone, "devone coefficients, unbounded and wrapped in the",
    "likelihood (no uniform(-pi, pi) prior or bound). \n")

```

### Reading the saved sampling diagnostics

Posterior summaries require the sampler to explore the fitted distributions reliably. The saved fits show no entries in the reported convergence-failure tables, but they also state that divergence information was not retained in the fit objects. An empty table therefore does not establish that there were zero divergences. Sampling diagnostics and the leave-one-out diagnostics below assess different aspects of reliability, and both matter when interpreting the comparison.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-025"
# The 1-component baseline runs at the stem's full fit budget (ITER/WARMUP).
# Its population mean sits on a near-flat gauge ridge (the
# population mean and the per-animal deviations are identified only
# in combination), and under the pre-alignment priors even the full
# cmdstan budget failed on it (rhat 1.034, ESS 322 for mu_pop, with
# 71% of transitions hitting the max treedepth limit). The aligned
# priors above are what let the gate clear at the full budget.
data_anchor <- as.numeric(mod_circular(circ_mean(df$direction)))
individual_anchor <- vapply(split(df$direction, df$animal), circ_mean, numeric(1))
anchor_offsets <- as.numeric(mod_circular(individual_anchor - data_anchor))
if (abs(data_anchor) >= pi - 0.2 || any(abs(anchor_offsets) >= pi - 0.5)) {
  ordered_means <- sort(individual_anchor)
  gaps <- diff(c(ordered_means, ordered_means[1] + 2 * pi))
  widest <- which.max(gaps)
  seam <- ordered_means[widest] + gaps[widest] / 2
  data_anchor <- as.numeric(mod_circular(seam + pi))
  anchor_offsets <- as.numeric(mod_circular(individual_anchor - data_anchor))
}
stopifnot(length(data_anchor) == uni_design$K_popone,
          length(anchor_offsets) == uni_design$K_devone,
          abs(data_anchor) < pi - 0.2, all(abs(anchor_offsets) < pi - 0.5))
mk_init <- function(anchor_seed) {
  set.seed(anchor_seed)
  j <- function(n) runif(n, -0.08, 0.08)
  list(b_popone = as.numeric(data_anchor + j(uni_design$K_popone)),
       b_devone = as.numeric(anchor_offsets + j(uni_design$K_devone)))
}
init_uni <- lapply(seq_len(CHAINS), function(k) mk_init(SEED + k))
set.seed(SEED)
fit_unimodal <- unwrap_load_fit_cache("locust_mix_unimodal_unbounded_v2", SEED, ITER, WARMUP)
if (is.null(fit_unimodal)) {
  fit_unimodal <- brm(uni_form, data = df, prior = uni_priors, stanvars = uni_stanvars,
    backend = "cmdstanr", chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP,
    cores = CHAINS, seed = SEED, init = init_uni,
    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.97, max_treedepth = 12))
  unwrap_save_fit_cache("locust_mix_unimodal_unbounded_v2", fit_unimodal, SEED, ITER, WARMUP)
}
state_unimodal <- extract_state(fit_unimodal, bimodal = FALSE)
summary_unimodal <- diagnose_fit(fit_unimodal, state_unimodal)
```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-026"
save_figure(trace_plot(state_unimodal,
  c("mu_pop", "mu_kappa", "kappa_pop", "kappa_sigma")), "unimodal_trace", 9, 5)
```

## Does a second component improve prediction?

Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO) approximates predicting each heading after leaving it out of the fit. The animal's other headings remain available, so this targets another heading from the observed animals. Prediction for an entirely new animal would require a different validation design.

The expected log predictive density (ELPD) adds these predictive contributions over headings. Higher values indicate better predictive performance under this comparison. The saved scores favor the two-component fit, while the animal panels show that the gain varies between individuals. Each animal's score is the **sum** of its heading contributions. Animals with more observations can therefore contribute more strongly to the total difference.

The total-score bars summarize uncertainty in the estimated predictive score. The current per-animal panels do not estimate uncertainty intervals; absent or zero-length bars should not be interpreted as certainty about an animal's contribution.

PSIS-LOO also reports Pareto-$k$ diagnostics, which identify headings for which its approximation may be unreliable. The saved results flag some headings in both notebook versions. Read the direction of the displayed comparison together with these warnings and the sampling diagnostics above. A numerical advantage in the saved plot does not by itself establish that the model comparison is reliable, or that a particular neural mechanism has been demonstrated.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-028"
loo_bimodal <- explicit_loo(state_bimodal)
loo_unimodal <- explicit_loo(state_unimodal, bimodal = FALSE)
models <- list(Bimodal = loo_bimodal, Unimodal = loo_unimodal)
elpd_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(name) {
  x <- models[[name]]
  data.frame(model = name, elpd = x$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"],
    se = x$estimates["elpd_loo", "SE"], max_pareto_k = max(x$diagnostics$pareto_k),
    n_pareto_k_gt_0.7 = sum(x$diagnostics$pareto_k > 0.7))
}))
delta_pointwise <- loo_bimodal$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - loo_unimodal$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
print(elpd_table)
print(data.frame(comparison = "Bimodal - Unimodal", delta_elpd = sum(delta_pointwise),
                 se = sqrt(length(delta_pointwise) * var(delta_pointwise))))
model_labels <- c(Bimodal = "Bimodal\n(Vec. encoding)",
                  Unimodal = "Unimodal\n(Optic flow)")
p_elpd <- elpd_comparison_plot(elpd_table)
save_figure(p_elpd, "locust_bimodal_unimodal_elpd", 6, 3)
```

```{r}
elpd_individual <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(num_individuals), function(i) {
  ii <- which(df$animal_id == i - 1L)
  data.frame(individual = i,
    bimodal = sum(loo_bimodal$pointwise[ii, "elpd_loo"]),
    unimodal = sum(loo_unimodal$pointwise[ii, "elpd_loo"]),
    delta = sum(delta_pointwise[ii]), se = 0)
}))
cat("Individual ELPD: bimodal better for", sum(elpd_individual$delta < 0),
    "of", num_individuals, "animals.\n")
p_elpd_ab <- elpd_individual_plot(elpd_individual, num_individuals)
save_figure(p_elpd_ab, "locust_elpd_by_individual_ab", 10, 12)
```

## Does the fitted density reproduce the directional pattern?

The next figures compare the mixture's fitted density with two descriptions of the observed headings: a circular histogram and a smoothed circular density estimate. These descriptions retain the full pattern around the circle, including multiple peaks that a single mean could conceal.

The saved figures show two broad concentrations near the lateral directions and less density near forward. The mixture reproduces that broad structure. This is the feature relevant to the biological question: the headings favor the two sides in this experimental arrangement. Agreement in the main peaks supports this description, while differences in peak widths, heights, and troughs show where the fitted distribution and observations differ.


The red curve summarizes the density obtained from the population parameters with all individual deviations set to zero. Its band shows posterior uncertainty in that fitted density. This population reference is different from averaging the fitted densities of the observed animals or predicting a new animal after allowing for individual variation.

For the observed-data estimates, a hierarchical bootstrap resamples animals and then headings within each selected animal. Each animal's density receives equal weight, so the longest recordings do not dominate the displayed population pattern. The histogram groups headings into angular bins; the von Mises kernel density estimate smooths them around the circle. Their bootstrap bands describe variation under this resampling procedure.

The model and bootstrap bands answer different uncertainty questions. The reference with individual deviations set to zero also differs from the observed density averaged across animals. Compare the broad directional structure with those distinctions in mind. The Cartesian and polar figures show the same comparison in different coordinates. A fuller check of the observed sample follows below, using replicated headings for each animal.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-032"
population_state <- list(muone = state_bimodal$pop_muone,
  mutwo = state_bimodal$pop_mutwo, kone = state_bimodal$pop_kone,
  ktwo = state_bimodal$pop_ktwo, weight = state_bimodal$pop_weight,
  eta = state_bimodal$pop_eta)
theta_grid <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 360L)
pop_mu <- rbind(as.numeric(population_state$muone), as.numeric(population_state$mutwo))
pop_kappa <- rbind(as.numeric(population_state$kone), as.numeric(population_state$ktwo))
pop_pdf <- mixture_grid(theta_grid, pop_mu, pop_kappa, as.numeric(population_state$weight))
stopifnot(identical(dim(pop_pdf), c(length(theta_grid), nrow(state_bimodal$draws))))
# Python population_density summarizes log density first, then exponentiates.
q_pop <- exp(t(apply(log(pop_pdf), 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))))
model_density <- data.frame(theta = theta_grid,
  low = q_pop[, 1], center = q_pop[, 2], high = q_pop[, 3])
rm(pop_pdf)
rows_by_animal <- split(seq_len(nrow(df)), df$animal)
bins <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 17L)
bin_width <- diff(bins)[1]
bin_id <- findInterval(wrap(df$direction), bins, rightmost.closed = TRUE)
stopifnot(all(bin_id >= 1L & bin_id <= 16L))
hist_kernel <- matrix(0, nrow = 16L, ncol = nrow(df))
hist_kernel[cbind(bin_id, seq_len(nrow(df)))] <- 1 / bin_width
# Each column is one observed heading's VM kernel on the theta grid.
kde_kernel <- kde_basis(theta_grid, df$direction, bw = 30)
boot_hist <- matrix(0, nrow = 16L, ncol = N_BOOTSTRAPS)
boot_kde <- matrix(0, nrow = length(theta_grid), ncol = N_BOOTSTRAPS)
set.seed(123)
for (b in seq_len(N_BOOTSTRAPS)) {
  selected <- sample.int(num_individuals, num_individuals, replace = TRUE)
  weights <- numeric(nrow(df))
  for (i in selected) {
    ii <- rows_by_animal[[i]]
    draw <- sample.int(length(ii), length(ii), replace = TRUE)
    weights[ii] <- weights[ii] + tabulate(draw, nbins = length(ii)) /
      (num_individuals * length(ii))
  }
  stopifnot(abs(sum(weights) - 1) < 1e-10)
  boot_hist[, b] <- as.numeric(hist_kernel %*% weights)
  boot_kde[, b] <- as.numeric(kde_kernel %*% weights)
}
bin_centers <- head(bins, -1L) + bin_width / 2
hist_density <- density_frame(bin_centers, boot_hist)
kde_density <- density_frame(theta_grid, boot_kde)
rm(hist_kernel, kde_kernel, boot_hist, boot_kde)
invisible(gc())
p_hist <- model_layer() +
  geom_errorbar(data = hist_density, aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), width = 0.06) +
  geom_point(data = hist_density, size = 1.5)
p_kde <- model_layer() +
  geom_ribbon(data = kde_density, aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), fill = "black", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(data = kde_density, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5)
p_validation_cartesian <- (p_hist / p_kde) | val_legend(framed = FALSE)
p_validation_cartesian <- p_validation_cartesian + plot_layout(widths = c(4, 1))
save_figure(p_validation_cartesian, "population_directional_validation_cartesian", 7, 7)
```

```{r}
p_validation_polar <- population_polar_plot(model_density, kde_density,
  hist_density)
save_figure(p_validation_polar, "population_directional_validation", 7, 7)
```

## How well does the mixture describe each animal?

The individual panels compare an animal's observed headings and bootstrap density with its fitted mixture density and posterior uncertainty. They reveal patterns that can disappear when animals are averaged together: differences in preferred direction, the relative prominence of the two components, and how concentrated the headings are.

A clear population pattern does not imply that every animal has two equally distinct peaks. Some individuals contribute too few headings to identify a detailed distribution, while others favor one component. Look for agreement in the locations and breadth of the main concentrations, and for headings that fall where the fitted density is low. These comparisons assess the description of the recorded animals rather than providing independent validation on new animals.


The component arrows summarize preferred directions, with lengths combining component weight and concentration through its mean resultant length. Their directions use wrapped arithmetic summaries of the sampled component angles, so they should be read alongside the full density bands, particularly if a component spans the angular boundary. Outward ticks mark observed headings; inward ticks emphasize observations assigned low fitted density. These annotations help locate disagreement, but the inward ticks are not a separate calibrated goodness-of-fit test.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-036"
ppc_layers <- individual_ppc_layers(state_bimodal, df, rows_by_animal,
  num_individuals, N_BOOT_KDE)
ppc_curves <- ppc_layers$curves
ppc_ticks <- ppc_layers$ticks
ppc_arrows <- ppc_layers$arrows
p_individual_ppc <- individual_ppc_plot(ppc_curves, ppc_ticks, ppc_arrows)
save_figure(p_individual_ppc, "locust_directional_individual_ppc", 14, 16)
```

### Could the fitted models generate similar heading patterns?

Posterior predictive simulation asks what another dataset could look like under a fitted model. For each replicate, we take one shared posterior draw, retain the fitted parameters of the 52 observed animals, and simulate the observed number of headings for each animal. The two-component model first chooses a component according to that animal's weight and then draws a heading from it. The single-component model draws from its one von Mises distribution.

We summarize the replicated headings with the same histogram and kernel density estimates used for the observations. Population curves average animal densities with equal weight. The colored bands therefore include both uncertainty in the fitted parameters and variation from generating a finite set of headings. They answer a different question from the earlier bands around an analytic fitted density. The black curves, points, and bands describe the observed-data bootstrap.

In the saved population figures, the two-component model reproduces the lateral peaks and the intervening trough more closely. The one-component model produces a broader pattern, with less pronounced peaks and more density between them. The individual grid shows where this difference is most apparent and where the models give similar descriptions. These are checks of marginal heading distributions for the observed animals; they do not test the timing of changes in direction. Interpret the one-component simulations with the sampling limitations already described.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "p3-ppc-draws"
set.seed(SEED + 1L)
ppc_bimodal <- predictive_checks(state_bimodal, "Bimodal", model_tag = 1L)
set.seed(SEED + 2L)
ppc_unimodal <- predictive_checks(state_unimodal, "Unimodal", model_tag = 2L)
```

```{r}
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Bimodal = ORANGE, Unimodal = BLUE)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Bimodal = ORANGE, Unimodal = BLUE)) +

  facet_grid(estimate ~ model) +

    caption = "Black: observed bootstrap. Colour: posterior predictive replicates.") +

save_figure(p_population_predictive, "population_predictive_both_models", 9, 7)
```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "p3-ppc-ind"
individual_predictive <- rbind(ppc_bimodal$individual, ppc_unimodal$individual)
individual_predictive$individual <- factor(individual_predictive$individual,
                                            levels = levels(ppc_curves$individual))
# Same radius convention as the other polar figures: density zero sits on

individual_predictive$r_center <- 1 + individual_predictive$center / peak_max_ppc
individual_predictive$r_high <- 1 + individual_predictive$high / peak_max_ppc

  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Bimodal = ORANGE, Unimodal = BLUE)) +
```

## Which directional prediction agrees with the fitted mixture?

We now evaluate the two-component mixture at the directions predicted by the competing accounts. For each posterior draw, the population parameters with individual deviations set to zero define

$$
f_0(y)=\omega_0\,\mathcal M(y\mid\mu_{0,1},\kappa_{0,1})
 +(1-\omega_0)\,\mathcal M(y\mid\mu_{0,2},\kappa_{0,2}).
$$

The forward and lateral comparisons are

$$
d_F=f_0(0),\qquad
d_L=\frac{f_0(-\pi/2)+f_0(+\pi/2)}{2}.
$$

These quantities are **densities per radian**. Averaging the two lateral values puts the lateral and forward comparisons on the same scale: both equal $1/(2\pi)\approx0.159$ under a uniform heading distribution. This avoids giving the lateral prediction a larger value simply because it specifies two directions. A probability of heading within a finite angular range would instead require integrating the density over that range.

The saved population panels place the lateral density at roughly 0.28 per radian and the forward density at roughly 0.08. The lateral value lies above the uniform reference and the forward value below it. Conditional on the fitted mixture, this supports the lateral directional prediction in this experimental setting. It does not give a posterior probability that one neural mechanism is true, and it is not a Bayes factor between mechanistic models.

The comparison is repeated with each animal's parameters to show variation around the shared pattern. The accompanying probability panel reports the fraction of posterior draws in which the animal's lateral average exceeds its forward density, $P(d_L>d_F\mid Y)$. Its meaning is specific to that density comparison. The reported 95% posterior intervals are calculated on the log-density scale and transformed back to the density scale.


### Reading the remaining hypothesis figures

The fixed-direction figures labeled “ELPD” summarize the **mean log density at each theory-predicted direction over posterior draws**. They are separate from the earlier PSIS-LOO comparison, which predicts omitted observations. For the lateral prediction, the density is averaged across the two directions before taking its logarithm.

The bars in these fixed-direction log-density figures are $1.96\,\mathrm{sd}(\log d)/\sqrt{S}$, using the raw number of posterior draws $S$. They are not posterior credible intervals and are not adjusted for the effective sample size of the chains. Their narrowness should therefore not be interpreted as little uncertainty in the animals' behavior or in the fitted density. Use the density panels' posterior intervals to examine parameter uncertainty.

The “pooled” row first averages individual log densities with equal animal weights within each draw. On the density scale, it consequently represents a geometric mean of individual densities. It differs from an arithmetic average of individual densities and from the separate population reference obtained by setting individual deviations to zero.

The final figures summarize how the component mean directions align with the predictions:

$$
A_F=\sum_{k=1}^{2}w_k\cos(\mu_k),\qquad
A_L=\sum_{k=1}^{2}w_k\cos\!\left[2(\mu_k-\pi/2)\right],
$$

where $w_1=\omega$ and $w_2=1-\omega$. The doubled angle in $A_L$ treats both lateral directions as aligned, so they reinforce each other instead of cancelling. These scores use component directions and weights but omit component concentration. A diffuse component can therefore have a high alignment score if its mean points toward the relevant direction. Read the scores as summaries of component orientation, not as heading consistency, mean resultant length, or probabilities. The zero reference on these score plots is also different from the uniform density reference in the preceding figures.

In the individual alignment figure, the accompanying probability panel reports $P(A_L>A_F\mid Y)$. It compares the alignment scores, whereas the earlier probability panel compares the densities through $P(d_L>d_F\mid Y)$.


```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-039"
hyp_pop <- hypothesis_arrays(population_state)
hyp_ind <- hypothesis_arrays(state_bimodal, clip = TRUE)
pop_density_table <- make_hyp_table(hyp_pop, "density")
print(pop_density_table)
save_figure(population_dots(pop_density_table, "Predictive density", 1 / (2 * pi),
  baseline_label = "Uniform"),
  "locust_directional_hypothesis_horizontal", 6, 3)
```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-040"
pop_elpd_table <- make_hyp_table(hyp_pop, "elpd")
print(pop_elpd_table)
save_figure(population_dots(pop_elpd_table, "Mean log predictive density at hypothesis",
  -log(2 * pi), baseline_label = "Uniform"),
  "locust_directional_hypothesis_horizontal_elpd", 6, 3)
```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-041"
individual_density_table <- make_hyp_table(hyp_ind, "density", pooled = TRUE)
pooled_row <- individual_density_table[individual_density_table$individual == "Pooled", ]
pooled_row <- pooled_row[order(individual_density_table$hypothesis), , drop = FALSE]
cat("Pooled row - Optic flow center:", signif(pooled_row$center[1], 3),
    "| Vec. encoding center:", signif(pooled_row$center[2], 3), "\n")
save_figure(individual_dots(individual_density_table, "Predictive density", 1 / (2 * pi)),
  "locust_directional_hypothesis_individual_ab", 10, 13)

```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-042"
individual_elpd_table <- make_hyp_table(hyp_ind, "elpd", pooled = TRUE)
pooled_row <- individual_elpd_table[individual_elpd_table$individual == "Pooled", ]
pooled_row <- pooled_row[order(individual_elpd_table$hypothesis), , drop = FALSE]
cat("Pooled row - Optic flow center:", signif(pooled_row$center[1], 3),
    "| Vec. encoding center:", signif(pooled_row$center[2], 3), "\n")
save_figure(individual_dots(individual_elpd_table, "Mean log predictive density at hypothesis", -log(2 * pi)),
  "locust_directional_hypothesis_individual_elpd_ab", 10, 13)

```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-043"
# Weight-only alignment is the source estimand; no A1(kappa) factor.
align_pop <- alignment_arrays(population_state)
align_ind <- alignment_arrays(state_bimodal)
pop_alignment_table <- make_hyp_table(align_pop, "alignment")
print(pop_alignment_table)
save_figure(population_dots(pop_alignment_table, "Posterior mean alignment", 0,
  invert = TRUE) +
              coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.05, 1)),
  "locust_directional_alignment_horizontal", 6, 3)
```

```{r}
#| cell-id: "locust-r-044"
individual_alignment_table <- make_hyp_table(align_ind, "alignment")
pooled_row <- individual_alignment_table[individual_alignment_table$individual == "Pooled", ]
pooled_row <- pooled_row[order(individual_alignment_table$hypothesis), , drop = FALSE]
cat("Pooled row - Optic flow center:", signif(pooled_row$center[1], 3),
    "| Vec. encoding center:", signif(pooled_row$center[2], 3), "\n")
save_figure(individual_dots(individual_alignment_table, "Posterior mean alignment", 0,
                            limits = c(-1, 1)),
  "locust_directional_alignment_individual_ab", 10, 13)

```

## What this example shows

The recorded headings have a strong lateral structure that a single circular mean would obscure. A hierarchical mixture makes that structure interpretable by separating component directions, concentration around those directions, and relative component use, while sharing information across animals with very unequal numbers of observations.

The saved mixture figures reproduce the broad lateral peaks, and its fitted population density is higher at the lateral predictions than at forward. This is consistent with the vectorial account's directional prediction in this experiment. The individual panels show variation around that pattern, rather than requiring every animal to express two equally clear peaks.

Predictive comparison, replicated-data checks, and evaluation at theory-predicted directions contribute different evidence. Their numerical interpretation remains subject to the sampling and leave-one-out diagnostics described above. The biological conclusion concerns the directional pattern under this task; these statistical models alone do not identify a unique neural mechanism.
